brief.notification_title: Nvidia CEO turmoil hits futures; Fed hike bets firm
brief.market_summary: The S&P 500 rose 1.31% on Wednesday to 7,619 and SMH gained 4.82%, both lifted by CoreWeave's results. That rally is being taken back this morning. S&P futures are down 0.46% and Nasdaq 100 futures 1.03%, because Nvidia is 6–9% lower pre-market after a WSJ report that its board is preparing to remove Jensen Huang. In rates, last week's hot CPI (core 0.3% vs 0.2% expected) has firmed up December hike bets. The 2-year rose 17bp on Tuesday to 4.73%, the 10-year sits at about 5.0%, the dollar is at a 19-month high and gold is below $4,000. Brent is at $92.31, down 6% on the week, after OPEC+ output jumped by more than 2M bpd and on hopes of peace in Iran and Ukraine. Bitcoin, at $72.7K, is near its lowest since August after five straight days of ETF outflows. Ether is at $2,015, just above our $2,000 backstop.
brief.since_last:
What's new since yesterday:
- **Nvidia governance.** WSJ/CNBC report the board met Wednesday to decide whether to remove Huang (n37, n49, n142). Separately, Washington is moving to tighten Nvidia's China exports (n56).
- **AI trade reversing.** Nebius fell about 10% after raising capex and giving a weak outlook (n2). CoreWeave and IREN are also lower (n43). AMD and Broadcom are up about 3%, so the selling is aimed at Nvidia rather than all of AI.
- **MSTR.** MSCI confirmed it will remove Strategy from its indexes, effective 30 Nov (n94).
- **Oil.** OPEC's report shows October output at about 97% of pre-war levels, and API reported a 9.0M bbl crude build against a 1.0M draw expected. Brent fell below $93.
- **Fed.** Speakers kept hike bets alive (n101). One report says December hike odds are at 100% (n156), and FXStreet says traders are weighing a half-point move (n106).

**Data caveats:**
- The Treasury cash market was closed Wednesday for Veterans Day, so treat Wednesday's yield prints in the snapshot as thin or stale.
- The calendar timestamps CPI as 11 Nov, but sources say it was released Tue 10 Nov.
- The snapshot is from 08:08 ET, before the 08:30 jobless claims. The "08:08 Asia" stamp in the header doesn't match the sources.

brief.instructor_take: Two different shocks are hitting at once, and you should keep them apart. The first is macro. Core CPI at 0.3% for a second month has turned a December hike into close to a certainty, and that is what lifts the dollar, sinks gold below $4,000 and drains crypto. The second is specific to one company: Nvidia may be losing its founder-CEO at the same moment Washington tightens its China exports. The crowd may treat Nvidia as a one-stock problem, but MarketWatch's "bank of Nvidia" piece (n11) makes the right point. Nvidia finances much of its own customer base, so a leadership vacuum is a supply-chain credit question, and that's why Nebius and CoreWeave are falling with it. On the other side, AMD and Broadcom rising tells me the market isn't selling AI demand. It's selling key-person risk. My stance is simple: over the next six days there are four binary events (AMAT and Cisco tonight, PPI tomorrow, the Huang decision, and Nvidia on the 17th), and with bills paying around 4.1–4.3% I'm paid to wait rather than guess. A less experienced investor will see Nvidia down 8% and call it a bargain. Without knowing who runs the company next week, you can't price it, and a dip you can't price isn't a bargain. I'd be wrong if AMAT guides strongly, the board resolves the Huang question quickly, and SMH reclaims $508. In that case I rebuild on the rules we already set, without chasing.

top_ideas.title: Stay out of semis until AMAT, Huang and Nvidia
top_ideas.one_liner: Don't buy the Nvidia gap; re-enter semis only on the set rules
top_ideas.thesis: Yesterday's avoid is working: SMH closed at 506.96, below the $513 we refused to chase, and will open lower with Nvidia down 6–9%. I'm adding a third condition to re-entry: the Huang leadership question has to be publicly resolved, on top of AMAT's guide and Nvidia's 17 Nov report.
top_ideas.reasoning: I'm applying event-risk sequencing. When several binary events are lined up close together, you wait for them to resolve rather than pay for the uncertainty. Nvidia is the largest SMH holding, and today it faces a governance risk you can't model, because nobody knows whether the board acts, who replaces Huang, or how hyperscaler relationships hold up. AMAT tonight is a separate test. Its $4.06 bar is nearly double last year's $2.17, and Washington's China tightening (n56, n134) puts its guide at risk. Nebius falling 10% on a revenue beat shows the market is punishing heavy capex right now, which is a late-cycle sign in a theme. A newer investor would buy the dip in Nvidia alone. I'd point out that SMH's 1-month return is -13.8% even after Wednesday's +4.8%, so the trend is still down. What would change my mind: AMAT beats and raises, the board confirms continuity or names a credible successor, and SMH closes Friday above $508.

top_ideas.title: Let the ETH trim rule run near the $2,000 backstop
top_ideas.one_liner: ETH is 1% above the $2,000 backstop; let the trim rule run
top_ideas.thesis: ETH has fallen 16.5% in a week to $2,015, so the $2,150/$2,200 limit sells have most likely not filled, and the $2,000 daily-close backstop is about to be tested. Flows and liquidity are still against it: five straight days of ETF outflows, $144.8M out of ETH funds Wednesday, and stablecoin supply down $14.2B over 30 days.
top_ideas.reasoning: I think in liquidity terms here. Crypto rallies need new dollars coming in, and right now they're leaving through ETF redemptions and a shrinking stablecoin float, the largest 30-day drop since 2022 (n72). Macro adds to it: a near-certain December hike and a 19-month high in the dollar lift the return on cash, which is what high-beta, no-yield assets compete with. ETH is underperforming BTC on the week (-16.5% vs -9.4%), so it's the weaker leg and the one to cut first. The discipline lesson matters more than the call. We set a backstop in advance so we don't have to decide under stress, and the worst thing to do now is lower the trigger because it's close. A less experienced investor reads the Fear index at 28 and the 'golden cross' talk (n77) as reasons to hold. Sentiment is a poor timing tool while flows are still negative. I'd change my mind if ETH reclaims $2,400 with three straight days of ETF inflows.

top_ideas.title: IEF second tranche only at the $90.60 limit
top_ideas.one_liner: Buy the second IEF half only at $90.60; cancel on hot core PPI
top_ideas.thesis: With the 10-year at about 5.0% (IEF 90.94), the second tranche stays at the $90.60 limit (about 5.04%), good through Friday. Today's 30-year auction or a hot PPI could push it there. Hikes that flatten the curve eventually cap long yields, but I want a better price and the PPI result before committing.
top_ideas.reasoning: The concept here is the bear flattener. After CPI, the 1-year rose 18bp but the 10-year only 10bp, which tells you the market reads more hikes as eventually slowing the economy. That's why intermediate duration at about 5% is a reasonable multi-month hold. Bloomberg reporting haven buying in long bonds on the Nvidia news (n76) shows Treasuries still work as a hedge against equity shocks, and that's the portfolio role I want from IEF. The risks are real. The 10-year auction drew a soft 2.46 bid-to-cover, and if a 50bp hike gets priced, yields across the curve move up together. That's why I set a limit instead of buying at market and attached a PPI cancellation rule. Many investors forget that a limit order is a way of saying in advance which price is worth the risk. Today's 30-year auction (last cleared at 5.618%) could tail and give us the fill. Core PPI at 0.5% or higher means the inflation impulse is broadening, and I'd step aside.

lesson.explanation: A bear flattener is when yields rise across the curve ('bear', since bond prices fall) and short-term yields rise more than long-term ones ('flattener'). It usually happens when markets expect the central bank to hike. Short maturities track the policy rate closely, while long maturities also price the growth slowdown those hikes may cause. For investors, it means front-end bonds take the policy shock, and the long end starts to act as a hedge against a later slowdown.
lesson.todays_example: On the official curve after the hot October CPI, the 1-year rose 18bp, the 2-year 17bp, the 10-year 10bp and the 30-year 9bp. 2s10s narrowed to +25bp. That's why we're adding 7–10 year duration (IEF) slowly at about 5% and keeping cash in bills (SGOV), rather than buying short notes whose yields still follow every hike.
